warnings: Quiz language appears sparse; make assessment prompts explicit.

improvement_notes: Replace or revise diagram.png if it is a generic left-to-right signal-flow schematic. The accompanying instruction to trace a signal is not well matched to this lesson’s force, contact, and friction model; the visual should instead label normal force, friction, weight, contact geometry, and actuator limits.
Use “quasi-static lift” or “slow, approximately constant-velocity lift” instead of “stationary lift” to avoid ambiguity about whether the object is being lifted or merely held.

State explicitly that the Coulomb friction inequality is a static no-slip condition and that the safety factor is an instructional design convention, not a guarantee of stability. The lesson already implies this, but one precise sentence would strengthen the foundation.

The explanation that centered contacts reduce twisting should be qualified further: torque depends on the center of mass, contact locations, force directions, and the object’s orientation, not simply visual centering.

Add a short answer key or instructor note for the main design challenge, especially because the optional unequal-force extension introduces a useful general formula that students should be able to verify.

The Python lab is strong, but the boolean scatter plot is a coarse threshold visualization. A second plot of friction capacity versus normal force, with the safety-adjusted load as a horizontal line, would make the physics more interpretable.
Reduce minor repetition among the assumptions, interpretation, common mistakes, and real-robot caveats. The content is valuable, but a premium lesson could be slightly shorter without losing rigor.
Consider adding one small numerical torque example. The lesson introduces torque correctly but does not let students calculate how an offset center of mass changes the grasp requirement.

Add an explicit accessibility note for the diagrams, such as identifying arrow direction and color-independent meaning in the surrounding prose. The existing alt text is generally strong, but the generic diagram alt text is not sufficiently instructional.
